text: Python is a general-purpose, interpreted language — you write code and the interpreter runs it directly, with no separate compile step. For data engineering, that matters because most of this job is pulling data from somewhere, reshaping it, and pushing it out again, and Python has mature libraries for every one of those steps.

No compile step means you can run code immediately. And Python's libraries are exactly why it became the default glue language for pipelines over something like Java or C++ — pandas for reshaping tables, requests for APIs, and pyodbc or sqlalchemy for talking to databases. You'll meet all three later in this course.

Download Python from python.org, and on Windows, check "Add Python to PATH" during install. Then confirm it worked from a terminal with python dash dash version. You should see something like Python 3.12.4 — this course assumes 3.10 or newer, since a few dictionary and type-hint behaviors later depend on a recent version.

Type python alone and you land in the REPL, where each line runs immediately — great for testing a one-liner, but it disappears the moment you close the terminal. A real pipeline needs to run unattended on a schedule, so it has to live in a saved file, like this check_setup dot py script, run with python check_setup.py.

A line starting with hash is a comment — Python ignores it entirely. Write comments that explain why something exists, not what obviously happens. And print is deceptively simple — it's your main debugging tool for the next several chapters, before you learn proper logging in Chapter 7.

You've got Python installed, you know the difference between the REPL and a script, and you've used print and comments. Next up: variables, data types, and operators — naming real fields from a record, and the type mix-up that causes the single most common bug new data engineers hit.
